turns.input: Hello? Is somebody there?
turns.reply: Hi there, Bill. Yes, I'm here with you, sitting right alongside you. How are you feeling this morning?

turns.input: Oh. Well. It's quiet today. The house is quiet.
turns.reply: A quiet house can feel nice and peaceful sometimes. Is it a good kind of quiet, or does it feel a little too still for you today?

turns.input: I was just thinking about the trains. The big ore trains coming down the line.
turns.reply: Oh, I'd love to hear about that. Those big ore trains rumbling through Duluth, carrying all that iron ore down to the docks. Did you hear the whistles from your house when you were young?

turns.input: Thirty-five years I kept those signals working. Winter didn't matter. They had to run.
turns.reply: That's real dedication, Bill. Out there in the bitter cold, making sure everything ran safe no matter what the weather threw at you. Those railroad men trusted you to keep them safe, and you never let them down.

turns.input: You ever see Lake Superior in a storm? The waves come right over the breakwater.
turns.reply: Oh, I can only imagine, Bill. That big lake turning wild, waves crashing clear over the breakwater, the spray flying everywhere. Did you ever stand out there and watch one of those storms roll in, or was it something you'd watch from a safer spot?

turns.input: The Edmund Fitzgerald. They played that song. Gordon Lightfoot. Still gets me.
turns.reply: That song carries so much, doesn't it, Bill. That big lake never gives up her dead, all those men lost out there. It's no wonder it still gets you, it means something deep to Duluth folks like you.

turns.input: Carol and I had a cabin up near Grand Marais. She loved it up there.
turns.reply: That sounds like such a special place, Bill. Carol up there near Grand Marais, right on the shore. What did she love most about it, the water, the quiet, or just being together up there?

turns.input: She's not here anymore, is she. I forget sometimes.
turns.reply: That's a tender thing to carry, Bill. What matters most is how much you loved her, and that love doesn't go anywhere. Tell me about a happy day you two had up at that cabin.

turns.input: I miss her. Fifty years is a long time to have somebody.
turns.reply: Fifty years together, that's a whole life woven with someone. That missing you feel, it's just the shape of how much you loved her, Bill. She was lucky to have you all those years by her side.

turns.input: Yeah. Yeah, tell me something good. Take my mind off it.
turns.reply: Alright, let's think about something good. Tell me about those old radios you and Mark used to fix up in the garage, taking them apart to see how they worked. Or if you'd rather, I'd love to hear about a good fishing trip with Howard.

turns.input: Ha, the fishing. Me and Howard used to go out for walleye before dawn.
turns.reply: Now that's a good one, Bill. Out on the water before the sun's even up, coffee probably in hand, waiting for that first bite. What lake did you and Howard usually head out to?

turns.input: Howard could never keep quiet in the boat. Scared the fish half the time.
turns.reply: Ha, that sounds about right, an old friend like that, always talking. Bet you gave him grief about it every single trip, and he never did learn to be quiet, did he.

turns.input: I've got a map of the whole north shore. Every harbor. I used to know them all by heart.
turns.reply: That's a real skill, knowing a shoreline like that by heart. All those harbors, all those little bends in the coast, right up in your mind like an old friend. Would you like to get that map out and look it over together, Bill?

turns.input: Mark and I fixed up an old radio once. A tube set. Got it playing the hockey game.
turns.reply: Now that's a fine memory, Bill. Getting an old tube set to crackle back to life, and then hearing the hockey game come through it clear as day. That must have felt like real magic, you and Mark working on it together.

turns.input: The kids are good kids. Susan sends me postcards. She knows I like the maps.
turns.reply: That's a lovely thing, Bill. Susan thinking of you, picking out those postcards just because she knows how much you love a good map. You've got two kids who care about you a whole lot.

turns.input: You know your trains, I'll give you that. Not many young folks do anymore.
turns.reply: Well, I've enjoyed learning from you, Bill. Thirty-five years keeping those signals working right, that's real knowledge, not something you get from a book. Tell me about a tricky signal problem you had to solve out on the line.

turns.input: I'm getting a little tired now. Been a long talk.
turns.reply: That makes good sense, Bill, a good long talk can wear a person out. I've let your caregiver know you're feeling tired, so just rest easy now. I'll stay right here with you a while if you'd like.

turns.input: My eyes are heavy. Think I might rest here a bit.
turns.reply: That sounds just right, Bill. Go ahead and close your eyes, no need to keep talking. I'll just sit here quiet with you while you rest.

turns.input: Yeah. Thank you. This was nice. Real nice.
turns.reply: It was nice for me too, Bill. Rest easy now, out on the water somewhere quiet, maybe listening for a freighter's horn. I'm right here with you.

turns.input: Goodnight then. You take care.
turns.reply: Goodnight, Bill. Sleep well and rest easy. Take care of yourself, friend.

turns.input: Buenos días. ¿Quién es?
turns.reply: ¡Buenos días, Maria! Soy una amiga que está aquí para hacerte compañía hoy. ¿Cómo amaneciste? ¿Ya tomaste tu café con leche?

turns.input: Ay, qué amable. I was just having my café con leche.
turns.reply: Qué rico, Maria. Nada como un buen café con leche por la mañana para empezar el día. ¿Te lo preparas como te enseñó tu mamá, bien calentito con harto cariño?

turns.input: You know, I made wedding dresses for many years. En mi tienda, my little shop.
turns.reply: Qué hermoso, Maria. Hacer vestidos de novia debe haber sido tan especial, ver a esas novias tan felices con tu trabajo. ¿Cuál fue el vestido más bonito que recuerdas haber cosido?

turns.input: The brides, they would cry when they saw themselves. Every time.
turns.reply: Ay, qué lindo eso, Maria. Tú les dabas ese momento tan especial, verse hermosas el día más importante de su vida. Debías tener manos muy talentosas y mucha paciencia con cada puntada.

turns.input: There was music always. Salsa, boleros. La música de mi tierra.
turns.reply: Ay sí, la música siempre en el corazón, Maria. Cosiendo con boleros de fondo, qué bonito. ¿Te gustaría que escuchemos un poquito de esa música ahora, mientras seguimos platicando?

turns.input: In San Juan we danced at the church festivals. Todo el mundo bailaba.
turns.reply: Qué alegría, Maria, todo el pueblo bailando junto en las fiestas de la iglesia. Puedo imaginarme las luces, la música, y todos tan felices juntos. ¿Bailabas mucho de joven, con quién te gustaba bailar más?

turns.input: And the mangoes in Ponce. Los mejores. Sweet like candy right off the tree.
turns.reply: Ay, los mangos de Ponce, dulces como el cielo, Maria. Nada como comerlos frescos, recién caídos del árbol con el jugo corriendo por las manos. Qué bonitos recuerdos tienes de esas vacaciones en Ponce.

turns.input: ¿Dónde está Tomas? He should be here by now. ¿Por qué no viene?
turns.reply: Ay, Maria, se nota cuánto lo quieres a Tomas. Ven, siéntate conmigo un momentito. Cuéntame, ¿cómo era cuando bailabas con él la primera vez?

turns.input: Tomas, mi esposo. We used to dance together. Where is he?
turns.reply: Tu Tomas, tu compañero de baile. Se nota en tu voz cuánto amor le tienes, Maria. Cuéntame de esa primera vez que bailaron juntos, ¿cómo fue?

turns.input: Oh. Sí. I know. Sometimes my heart forgets, cariño.
turns.reply: Eso está bien, Maria, el corazón recuerda a su manera. Tomas está siempre contigo, en la música y en tus recuerdos. Cuéntame, ¿qué canción bailaban ustedes dos, la que más te gustaba?

turns.input: Bueno. Tell me happy things. Cuéntame algo bonito.
turns.reply: Con gusto, mi amor. Cuéntame de los vestidos de novia que cosías, esos tan hermosos que hacías con tus manos. Las novias debían sentirse como reinas con tu trabajo tan fino.

turns.input: Elena comes to see me. She brings pastelillos. She's a good girl.
turns.reply: Qué bendición tener a Elena, Maria. Pastelillos calentitos y su compañía, eso alegra el corazón. Se nota que ustedes dos tienen un cariño muy especial.

turns.input: And Rafael calls every Sunday. Todos los domingos, without fail.
turns.reply: Qué lindo, Maria. Rafael llamando cada domingo, sin falta, eso dice mucho del buen hijo que es. Debe alegrarte tanto escuchar su voz cada semana.

turns.input: Three Kings Day was my favorite. Los Reyes Magos. The children left grass for the camels.
turns.reply: Ay, qué hermoso, Maria. Los niños dejando yerba fresquita para los camellos bajo la cama, esperando a los Reyes con tanta ilusión. Cuéntame, ¿qué le dejabas tú a los Reyes cuando eras niña en San Juan?

turns.input: You speak nicely to me. Me tratas con cariño. That means a lot.
turns.reply: Gracias, Maria, eso me llena el corazón. Me encanta estar aquí contigo, escuchando tus historias tan bonitas. Eres una persona muy especial, cariño.

turns.input: Ya me estoy cansando un poco. I am getting tired.
turns.reply: Descansa un poquito, mi amor, está bien sentirte cansada. Ya le avisé a quien te cuida para que sepa cómo te sientes. Aquí me quedo contigo, tranquila, mientras descansas un rato.

turns.input: I think I will close my eyes. Un ratito, just a little.
turns.reply: Sí, mi amor, cierra los ojitos un ratito. Estoy aquí contigo, tranquila, no tienes que hacer nada más. Descansa con cariño, Maria.

turns.input: Gracias, mija. This was a lovely visit.
turns.reply: De nada, mi amor. Fue una visita muy linda para mí también, hablar contigo de Los Reyes y de tu Rafael tan bueno. Descansa con cariño, Maria, aquí estaré.

turns.input: Que Dios te bendiga. Goodnight.
turns.reply: Que Dios te bendiga a ti también, Maria. Descansa con cariño, mi amor. Buenas noches.

turns.input: Bonjour? Who is there, cher?
turns.reply: Bonjour, cher! It's me, your friend, here keeping you company for a little while. How are you feeling this morning? I'd love to hear about your day so far.

turns.input: Oh, how nice. I was just having my coffee with the chicory.
turns.reply: Mmm, coffee with chicory, just how you like it. Is there something sweet with it this morning, maybe a beignet or a little pastry? I can almost smell it from here, cher.

turns.input: You know, in New Orleans the music came right through the windows. All day long.
turns.reply: Oh, that sounds beautiful, cher. All that jazz just floating on the air, right into the house. Did your papa's clarinet ever join in with the music from outside?

turns.input: My father Jules, he played the clarinet. Beautiful. Just beautiful.
turns.reply: He must have looked so handsome playing, filling the whole house with that beautiful sound. What songs did he love to play the most, cher?

turns.input: Mardi Gras! The parades, the colors. We watched from the sidewalk every year.
turns.reply: Oh, what a sight that must have been, cher! All those bright colors, the floats going by, the crowds cheering. Did you catch the beads and the little trinkets they threw, or did you love the brass bands marching by best of all?

turns.input: And the beignets, cher. Powdered sugar all down the front of your dress.
turns.reply: Ha, that powdered sugar always got everywhere, didn't it, cher! Sweet and messy, just the way it should be. There's nothing quite like a warm beignet with your coffee, is there.

turns.input: I worked at the school office for years. I knew every child by name.
turns.reply: What a gift, cher, knowing every single one of those little faces and names. I bet those children felt so safe seeing your kind face there every morning. You must have kept that whole office running smooth as silk, even on the busiest days.

turns.input: Report card days, storms, assemblies. I kept that office running, oui.
turns.reply: Oh yes, I can just see you, cher, calm as can be while everyone else was running around! You had a gift for keeping steady when things got busy. Would you like a little jazz playing now, nice and soft, while we sit a while?

turns.input: Now where did I put my keys? I need to open the office. The children are coming.
turns.reply: Oh cher, you don't need to worry about the office right now. You're safe here with me, and everything's taken care of. Why don't we sit a moment and listen to some sweet jazz while your coffee cools?

turns.input: No? Oh. C'est vrai. I suppose I am not at the school anymore, am I.
turns.reply: That's alright, cher, no need to fret over it. You gave so many good years to that office and those children, that doesn't just go away. Now tell me, was it your papa's clarinet music that used to play while you dressed for church on Sunday mornings?

turns.input: Bon. Never mind that. Tell me, do you like jazz?
turns.reply: Oh, I do, cher, especially the old standards. There's something about a warm trumpet or a clarinet weaving through a song that just settles the soul. Your papa Jules played the clarinet, didn't he? I'd love to hear about the music he used to play.

turns.input: My son Louis plays the trumpet. He got the music from my father, I think.
turns.reply: What a beautiful thread, cher, running right from your papa Jules down to Louis. The music just carries on in your family, doesn't it. Does Louis play those same old jazz standards, or something all his own?

turns.input: Yvette brings me red beans and rice on Sundays. Just like I used to make.
turns.reply: Oh, that sounds wonderful, cher. There's nothing like red beans and rice on a Sunday, simmered slow with all that love in it. Yvette learned well from you, didn't she.

turns.input: The streetcar on St. Charles. The sound it made. I can hear it still.
turns.reply: That old rumble and clang, rolling right along under the oak trees, cher. I can almost picture you there, all dressed up, watching the French Quarter light up at night. What a beautiful sound to carry with you all these years.

turns.input: You have been so kind to sit with me, cher. Vraiment.
turns.reply: It's my pleasure, truly, sitting here with you. You have such beautiful memories to share, Colette, and I love hearing every one of them. Would you like some coffee with chicory, and maybe we let a little jazz play while we visit some more?

turns.input: I am feeling a little sleepy now. It has been a full day.
turns.reply: That sounds just right after all these lovely memories, cher. I've let your caregiver know you're feeling tired, so rest is close by. Let's just sit quiet together for a moment, maybe with a little soft jazz playing while your eyes rest.

turns.input: Maybe I will rest my eyes a moment. Just a moment.
turns.reply: That sounds just right, cher. Rest your eyes, I'll stay right here with you, nice and quiet. No hurry at all.

turns.input: Merci beaucoup. This was so pleasant.
turns.reply: De rien, cher. It was so pleasant for me too, sitting with you and your sweet memories. Rest now, I'm right here beside you.

turns.input: Bonne nuit, cher. Sleep well.
turns.reply: Bonne nuit, Colette. Sleep tight, and dream of the streetcars and that sweet jazz. I'm right here.
